THE ART OF EFFORT: Philosophy and Intellectual Overcoming

The video combines mythology and philosophy to respond to what makes a life successful. It goes through the choice of Ulysses on the island of Calipso, the eudaimonia of Aristotle and the firmness that the video connects to Nietzsche, and ends in the brio: the refusal to be defeated by a difficult text.

The question: what makes a life successful

The video proposes to refuse passive comfort and accept intellectual friction as a way to find a purpose 00:14. The question that guides analysis is the oldest of all: what really matters in life 00:30.

Ulysses and the island of Calipso

Na Odyssey, of Homer, Ulysses stays seven years stuck on an island with the goddess Calipso 00:48. The island has all the comfort, but every night he goes to the beach crying of homesickness 01:06.

Calipso offers him immortality, and Ulysses refuses 01:17. He prefers to grow old and die as long as it is in Ithaca, his land 01:25. The video summarizes the choice like this: Better to be a mortal man in the right place than a god in the wrong place 01:34. There's no real success in spending your life standing where the tide left us. 01:41.

Aristotle's Eudaimony

Around 350 B.C., Aristotle defined the purpose of life, and for him success has no relation to passive comfort 01:51. The word he uses is idaimony: the active realization of their own talents, the happiness that comes from seeking excellence and developing their own nature altogether 02:04.

The video compares this to a tree change on fertile soil, which needs to grow roots, grow to maximum height and bear fruit 02:25. With people it is the same: there is an ethical commitment not to atrophy growth itself and to go as far as possible with the resources and intelligence we already have 02:36.

The firmness: after finding out, do not back down

The third point part of a phrase of popular wisdom: "It takes as long as it takes to realize what you want from existence, but when you realize it, don't back down on any pretext." 02:47. Discovering the purpose requires patience; defending the purpose requires an almost stubborn conviction 02:58.

For the video, the phrase echoes Nietzsche's philosophy, mainly in So spoke Zarathustra: when the person understands who he is, he advances, and does not go back nor to take impulse 03:07. The world will always put obstacles and voices that try to dissuade those who seek something big, and against this friction retreat is not an option 03:35.

The brio test

What sustains this determination is brio: a moral unconformism, a pride that says "eu I refuse to accept my own ignorance" 03:59. It is the discipline of not feeding the mind only with superficial information and easy to swallow 04:13.

Improving reasoning wears out, because it forces you to face hard texts from the front 04:23. The video gives examples:

  • read the ideas of Immanuel Kant until breaking the barrier of understanding 04:30;
  • to use shame constructively to dissect Pierre Bourdieu's theses by refusing to be less intelligent than the text 04:37;
  • remember that Pythagoras, starting almost from scratch, unveiled the relationships of the triangle, and that today, with so much information available, there is no excuse to claim inability 04:50.

Spending one morning rereading 30 times the same difficult paragraph may seem absurd, but the video treats it as a source of pride, not as punishment. 05:04. It is to look at the text and say: "eu will never be defeated by a mere set of words" 05:20.

The Art of Effort

The conclusion is that excellence belongs to those who reject the shallow waters and the misleading ease of Calipso Island. 05:30. It belongs to those who discover their own purpose, take control of their own intelligence and face intellectual friction with brio 05:41. It all depends on sustaining the discipline of effort to the end 05:51.

The video closes with a question for the viewer: what is the intellectual barrier that will not defeat us today 05:54?

Frequently Asked Questions

What is eudaimonia?

It is the term Aristotle uses for the ultimate purpose of life: the active realization of his own talents, the happiness that comes from seeking excellence 02:04.

Why does Ulysses refuse immortality?

Because he would rather be mortal in his own land, Ithaca, than immortal in the wrong place. 01:25.

What does the video call brio?

A moral unconformism, the pride of refusing to accept one's own ignorance before a text or a difficult idea 03:59.

Reviewed by Maurício Yokoyama Issei in 13 November 2026.

About the video

Have you ever felt like giving up when facing a difficult book or an intellectual challenge? In a world dominated by superficial content and ready answers, true mental strength is becoming a rarity.

In this explanatory video, we unite great lessons from classical mythology and Western philosophy to answer two fundamental questions: **What makes a life truly good?** and **How to develop the intellectual musculature never to back away from the difficult?**

Learn from the wise choice of Ulysses by refusing immortality on the island of Calipso to return to its right place (Itaca), understand the search for excellence (*eudaimony*) in Aristotle and discover Nietzsche's unwavering determination. Finally, face the test of the brio** — the unconformism that prevents us from accepting cognitive defeat before dense texts such as those of Kant and Bourdieu.

Put blood in your veins, refuse mediocrity and discover the power of deliberate effort.
